title: I don’t expect superposition in transformer MLP neurons
abstract: I currently believe that in a typical (well trained and under-parametrized) transformer model, there is something like superposition-type compression in the residual stream, but not in the MLP neurons. By "superposition-type compression", I mean some way of storing extra features using the fact that you can have almost orthogonal directions embedded in . [1] I've included the caveats "well trained and under-parametrized [2] " because I'm talking about networks that are at or close to full capacity. If the network is big enough (or just doesn't learn that many circuits for training reasons) then there is no need for compression, and therefore no need for superposition. [3] Why I believe this: [4] Having superposition everywhere causes too much noise from interference. There is much more need for compression in the residual stream. Compensating using some error correction is probably not worth it.

title: Returning to the Neuron Basis for Interpretability, Part 2: Using Neurons For Safety Applications
abstract: In a companion piece, we argue that individual neurons in language models are easier to interpret than earlier work has assumed. Here we see whether they could be useful for safety work. In open-weight models, we select neurons by what makes them fire and what they contribute to a model’s output. These neurons generally detect harmful text better than keyword or similarity search, though usually less well than classifiers trained on labeled examples, and they steer a model’s behavior about as well as trained methods. They also help an auditor find hidden behaviors in finetuned models. Finally, we find that most of the “unlearning” methods we tested appear to hide hazardous knowledge rather than remove it, and neurons help show how.

title: General-Purpose AI and the Future of Drone Autonomy in Contested Environments
abstract: When and how general-purpose AI could enable autonomous drones to operate in contested environments. The choices California makes while implementing its frontier AI law have ramifications for AI governance in the United States and around the world. A software-driven intelligence explosion is plausible but uncertain. Recommendations to strengthen how developers of advanced AI models assess, mitigate, and report biological risks under the EU AI Act. An intelligence explosion would compress years of progress into months and create urgent challenges for oversight, control, and governance. Embedded assessments can enable deeper and more flexible assessments of risks that depend on internal systems and practices. How to ensure AI safety incidents are identified, investigated, and used to improve safety across the industry. Developers rely on model-level, deployment-level, and governance-level interventions to address extreme misuse risks. Policymakers should complement biosecurity measures with stronger biosafety systems.

title: Interpreting a recent acceleration in pretraining loss
abstract: OpenAI recently published the base-model log-perplexity of 13 models it has trained since GPT-3.5, measured on a fixed held-out dataset sourced from its own codebase. It shows a very striking acceleration in pretraining loss: since early 2026, it has been falling about seven times faster than it was from 2022 through 2025. If the current pace holds, OpenAI would cover the drop in log-perplexity from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4.1, which took three years, in about six and a half months. This acceleration is even more striking because progress in loss should get harder over time: text is never perfectly predictable, so the loss can’t fall below some floor, and gains typically become smaller as models approach it.

title: Comparing AI R&D compute caps and deployment lags
abstract: I’m publishing this a bit rougher than usual because it’s very pertinent to Evan Hubinger’s recent shortform , which advocates for blocking internal deployment as a pacing mechanism over compute reallocation (he mostly discusses it in the context of a risk-assessment-based regime, while this post discusses the policies standalone). (see my response to Evan which also summarizes this post.) I compare 2 classes of policies: AI R&D compute cap : A cap on the percentage of compute used for capabilities R&D, as proposed at pacing-ai.com . Deployment lags/freezes: An X-month lag means that you have to use models X months old for AI R&D (or, AIs at most as capable as the AIs you trained X months ago). [1] A freeze means you pick a capability level above which you can’t use models to do AI R&D. I sometimes separate out internal-only lags/freezes from internal+external (“uniform”) ones.

title: The Accountable Agents Framework (AAF)
abstract: The Accountable Agents Framework (AAF) AI agents are becoming ubiquitous online, but there is no reliable way to identify who is responsible for their actions. This creates an accountability gap and increases hesitation around agent adoption in the economy and society. To help address this challenge, we introduce the Accountable Agents Framework (AAF), a protocol-agnostic framework that uses privacy-preserving IDs to link agents to their principals, such as a legal person. Directories verify principals’ identities and issue IDs, allowing agents to make verifiable claims about themselves as they transact. IDs are pseudonymous, revealing nothing about agents on their own, but if an agent causes harm, directories can deanonymize its principal according to an established process. Services can then more safely engage in transactions with agents that present a verified ID, since harm caused by such agents can be more reliably traced back to their principal.

title: Aligning Judge Models to Be Logically Consistent Multi-Rule Interpreters
abstract: Aligning Judge Models to Be Logically Consistent Multi-Rule Interpreters Technical governance of AI models will soon require them to reason over and follow thousands of rules from different jurisdictions. However, as we show in this work, presenting an entire ruleset to a judge model---rather than asking it to judge one rule at a time---changes the way the model interprets the requirements, making it reach conclusions that conflict with its rule-by-rule judgments. We call this challenge multi-rule inconsistency and find that models are more lenient when judging rules embedded within the full ruleset than when judging rules separately. For example, we find that when a safety-critical rule prohibiting a model from pursuing objectives other than those it was given appears in a larger ruleset, all tested judge models are less likely to deem it violated.

title: AI R&D-relevant model capabilities are improving rapidly and are getting harder to measure
abstract: Contents Overview 1 Background 2 Methodology 3 Results 4 Robustness Checks 5 Discussion 6 Acknowledgments Appendices A Difficulty Estimation and Baselining B Time Horizon Diagnostics C MCI Modelling Methodology D Limitations of IRT E MCI Robustness Checks F Estimating Lifecycle Cost for Tasks G Data Integrity and Reward Hacking H Changes in Capability Growth Rates I Inference Scaling J Swarm Experiments K Al Zimmermann's Programming Contests L Budget NanoGPT M Making METR tasks N Earthborne Rangers and Continual Learning O Qualitative and External Evidence on Models’ Strengths and Limitations Overview This post presents evidence from our capability evaluations of public models relevant to AI R&D acceleration, up to Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. We remain significantly uncertain about central questions, including (1) what capabilities are in practice necessary for drastic acceleration, and (2) how quickly relevant model capabilities are improving.
